sandhi.note: The final t stays unvoiced before p; the words are only written together.
Visarga after ai, before the voiced n, appears as r.

morph.note: Perfect ātmanepada of √नी: reduplication नि- and the root before the ending as -न्य- (नि-न्य्-ए). With यमक्षयम् it is the idiom ‘led to Yama’s house’, i.e. killed.
A kṛt formation with दुस्: दुःखेन ध्रियते ‘held back with difficulty’ — ‘irresistible’. Used as a name.
Periphrastic perfect of the causative (see 3.12): ‘made (the head) fall from the body’.

mantras.anvaya: (देवी) असिना बिडालस्य शिरः कायात् वै पातयामास। दुर्धरं दुर्मुखं च उभौ शरैः यमक्षयं निन्ये।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences with the Goddess as understood subject: object with its genitive and an ablative of separation; then two objects summed up by उभौ, an instrument and a goal.
mantras.lit: With the sword she indeed made Biḍāla’s head fall from his body; Durdhara and Durmukha, both, she led with arrows to the abode of Yama.
mantras.tr: With her sword she struck Biḍāla’s head from his body, and with her arrows she sent both Durdhara and Durmukha to the house of Death.

comm.t: The catalogue ends. Biḍāla was named among the commanders at 2.44 (बिडालाख्यः); Durdhara and Durmukha appear here for the first time. With them the named generals are all dead, and Mahiṣa must come himself (3.21).

samasa.literal: the asura who is a buffalo
samasa.alt: Also analysed as a madhyamapadalopī compound, महिषरूपः असुरः ‘the asura in buffalo form’; the karmadhāraya is simpler and fits the verse, which names his buffalo form separately.

morph.note: Passive present participle (क्षीय- + -मान, with ṇ after ī and y) in a locative absolute: ‘while his own army was being destroyed’.
Periphrastic perfect of the causative त्रासय- ‘make tremble’ (√त्रस् + णिच्, with vṛddhi a → ā).
Taddhita with vṛddhi of the first syllable (म → मा): ‘pertaining to a buffalo’. With स्वरूपेण, ‘in his own buffalo shape’.

mantras.anvaya: एवं स्वसैन्ये संक्षीयमाणे तु महिषासुरः माहिषेण स्वरूपेण तान् गणान् त्रासयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: A locative absolute (स्वसैन्ये संक्षीयमाणे) sets the time; the main clause has subject, instrumental of manner, object and the causative perfect.
mantras.lit: As his own army was thus being destroyed, Mahiṣāsura, in his own buffalo form, terrified those hosts.
mantras.tr: As his army wasted away, Mahiṣāsura himself, in his own buffalo shape, fell upon the Goddess’s hosts and struck terror into them.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Fell upon’ anticipates 3.22–23; ‘the Goddess’s hosts’ makes explicit who तान् गणान् are.

comm.t: Mahiṣa himself enters the battle. The gaṇas he terrifies are the hosts born from the Goddess’s breaths (2.52–53).

The phrase माहिषेण स्वरूपेण ‘in his own buffalo form’ marks the buffalo as Mahiṣa’s native shape. The other forms he takes later — lion, man with a sword, elephant (3.30–32) — are assumed, and at 3.33 he takes the buffalo body again.

sandhi.type: no change; n + c inside the pronoun
sandhi.note: The t of चित् stays before t. Inside the pronoun, कान् + चित् → कांश्चित्: n before c becomes anusvāra with an inserted ś.
Visarga before t becomes s; ā + a → ā.

sandhi.type: consonant sandhi (n + c, n + ś); vowel sandhi
sandhi.note: -आन् + च → -आंश्च. च + अन्यान् → चान्यान्. Before ś a final n optionally takes an inserted t (a rule not in our list); the n becomes ñ and the ś after the stop becomes ch: अन्यान् + शृङ्गाभ्याम् → अन्याञ्छृङ्गाभ्याम्. The Gita Press spells this sandhi out; GRETIL and Freund leave it unapplied (चान्यान्शृङ्गाभ्यां) — an orthographic variant (corrections.json).

samasa.literal: by a blow of the snout

morph.note: The indefinite pronoun declines in its first part (कश्चित्, कांश्चित्, केचित्): accusative plural ‘some’. कांश्चित् … अपरान् … अन्यान् distribute the victims: ‘some … others … others’.
Past participle of the causative दारय- (वि + √दॄ): ‘made to burst, ripped open’.
Instrumental dual: the buffalo’s pair of horns.

mantras.anvaya: कांश्चित् तुण्डप्रहारेण, तथा अपरान् खुरक्षेपैः, अन्यान् च लाङ्गूलताडितान्, (अन्यान्) च शृङ्गाभ्यां विदारितान् (पातयामास, 3.23)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A verse without a verb: four groups of victims in the accusative, each with how Mahiṣa struck them. The verb पातयामास comes in 3.23.
mantras.lit: Some with blows of his muzzle, likewise others with kicks of his hooves, and others lashed by his tail, and (others) torn open with his two horns —
mantras.tr: Some he struck down with blows of his muzzle, others with his hooves; others he lashed with his tail, and others he ripped open with his horns —
mantras.tr_note: The verse continues into 3.23, whose verb पातयामास (‘he felled’) is anticipated here as ‘struck down’.

comm.t: Mahiṣa fights as a buffalo, with every part of the animal: muzzle, hooves, tail, horns. The sentence runs on into 3.23, where the verb (‘he felled them on the ground’) finally comes.
